    Flygon Flow

    Flygon Flow keeps a MindMap (people, entities and ideas; called charts in the API), a product timeline, a DevOps board and AgentFlow (agents and workflows) in one workspace per environment. People use the web app. Agents use the same operations through the REST API, the MCP server or the CLI, authenticated with a personal API key (flow_…).

    Using the API

    Every operation is an HTTP call under the base URL of your Flow server:

    curl -sS "$FLOW_URL/api/v1/envs/$FLOW_ENV/cards" -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLOW_API_KEY"

    Keys look like flow_… and carry a scope: read (list and get), write (create, update and move) or admin (keys, sharing and environments). The OpenAPI document is at /api/v1/openapi.json. Errors come back with an HTTP status plus a code and a message. Path parameters such as {env} are filled from the input. Any other input is sent as the query string for GET and DELETE, or as the JSON body otherwise.

    Environments2 operationsMindMap charts1 operationNodes5 operationsEdges3 operationsProjects3 operationsTimeline4 operationsDevOps cards5 operationsLabels2 operationsAgentFlow agents8 operationsAgentFlow workflows4 operationsSearch1 operation

    Environments

    An environment is one workspace: its charts, projects, timeline and DevOps board, plus a record of who owns it.

    {"id": "acme-hq", "name": "Acme HQ", "ownerEmail": "owner@example.com", "visibility": "private", "members": []}
    • Every user starts in a new, empty, private environment. They can create more, rename them and archive them from Settings › Environment. Archiving hides an environment and keeps its data.
    • Isolation. A private environment can only be seen by its owner and its members. Anyone else gets 404, so the server does not even confirm that it exists. Anyone signed in can read a public environment, but only its owner can write to it.
    • Every API operation that touches workspace data is scoped to one environment through the {env} path segment. The server runs the read or write check before it touches any data.
    • Data saved before environments existed belongs to the instance's default environment.

    MindMap (charts)

    The app's MindMap tab is a free-form canvas of cards joined by edges. The API calls each mind map a chart (charts.list, nodes.*, edges.*). A workspace can hold several charts; one of them is active. In the app, right-clicking a card, a connection or empty canvas opens a menu of the actions that apply there.

    • Card types: entity (a company or organisation), person, area (a project area that groups cards inside it) and note.
    • Edge types: ownership is a solid arrow that can carry a percentage from 0 to 100, or "" when the percentage is unknown. group is a dashed line that means grouping only.
    • Cards snap to a 16px grid and can be resized. Moving an area also moves every card that sits fully inside it.
    • A person card can have a photo (image: an https:// URL, or a data:image/png|jpeg|webp;base64, URL of at most 61,440 characters) and an email (email, up to 200 characters, stored lower-case). In the app, the person's side panel can upload a photo (cropped to a 128px square), remove it, or Use my photo to take your account photo and email. A person whose email is yours shows your account photo until they get one of their own; so does a person with no email who is the only person in the workspace with your account name (matched ignoring case and extra spaces). This is me (shown when you are signed in and the person has no email) sets their email to yours, so they keep showing your live account photo. Matching only changes what is displayed: nothing is saved until you choose one of these buttons. The photo then appears wherever that person does: their card, DevOps assignee bubbles, pickers and AgentFlow supervisor badges. Invalid values, and photos or emails on other card types, are dropped.
    • Sharing a person shares their photo with whoever can see the card, but never their email.
    • Selecting an entity or area shows its project strip: the projects placed under it, their next timeline item, backlog counts and open DevOps cards.
    {"id": "c1", "name": "Acme · structure",
 "nodes": [{"id": "acme", "name": "Acme Holdings", "type": "entity", "x": 400, "y": 0},
           {"id": "rivera", "name": "Sam Rivera", "type": "person", "x": 320, "y": 144}],
 "edges": [{"id": "o1", "from": "rivera", "to": "acme", "type": "ownership", "percent": "60"}]}

    Validation is strict: ids must be unique, every edge must join two existing cards, and a card cannot connect to itself.

    Timeline

    The timeline holds dated items that are tagged with projects.

    • Item kinds: feature, milestone, release, deadline, project, phase, event.
    • Status: planned, active, risk, blocked, done, cancelled. Priority (high, medium, low) is optional.
    • start is YYYY-MM-DD, or empty for an unscheduled backlog item that appears only on the Board and List views. end is optional and never earlier than start.
    • A feature can target a release by title. The release then lists the items that target it and how many of them are done.
    • Projects are coloured tags {id, name, color, entity}. A project can sit under a chart entity or area through entity.
    • Views: Timeline (Gantt), Calendar, List and Board (a kanban by status). Filtered items can be exported as .ics.

    DevOps board and gates

    The DevOps board is a card board. Each card has an auto-incrementing #number.

    Columns, in order: requests (Requests / Sprinted, where new cards land), doing, blocked, uat, done, then the two backlogs must (Must Have) and nice (Nice to Have).

    A card holds title, description, column, project, labels[], points, due, assignees[{node, role}], checklist[{text, done}], links[{kind, url}], item and the created / updated / moved timestamps. Assignee roles are developer, tester and requester, and each assignee is a person card on the chart. Link kinds are pr, commit and url. item links the card to a timeline item. Responses also list agents, the AgentFlow agents the card is delegated to (see AgentFlow: delegation and the work queue).

    Gates

    Some moves need a confirmation or a decision. The app asks for it, and API callers must provide it explicitly:

    MoveGate
    UAT → Done with Approvenone (approval is the gate)
    anything else → doneconfirm-done
    done → anythingconfirm-reopen (reopen)
    → doing with no developerpick-dev: choose who develops it

    Labels have a section (priority, urgency, area, topic, other) and a colour key. Due dates turn amber two days before they are due and red once they are overdue.

    Agent inbox

    Agents can add or update projects, labels, timeline items and cards by dropping a JSON patch into the inbox. The open app picks the patch up within about 20 seconds and merges it as one undoable step.

    {"source": "Claude", "env": "acme-hq", "ops": [
  {"op": "upsertProject", "name": "Launch", "color": "#7cb980"},
  {"op": "upsertCard", "title": "Write release notes", "project": "Launch", "column": "requests", "labels": ["High"]},
  {"op": "patchCard", "number": 12, "column": "uat"}
]}
    • Ops: upsertProject, upsertLabel, upsertItem, upsertCard, patchCard.
    • References use names: a project by name, an assignee by the name of a person card, an item or release by title, and a label by id or name.
    • Safety: ops only add or update and never delete. Lists only grow. A field a human changed after the patch was written is kept, and the merge notes it. Applying the same patch again changes nothing.
    • CLI: node tools/inbox.mjs add|check|list|requeue.

    The token API is the direct way to make changes. The inbox suits agents that cannot hold a token, or changes a human should be able to undo in one click.

    Sync

    The server is the source of truth. Each environment's workspace is stored with a revision number, and the browser keeps an offline cache.

    • GET /api/workspace?env=<id> returns {rev, data}. PUT with {baseRev, data} saves the workspace when baseRev is still current.
    • If the workspace has moved on, the save gets 409 along with the newer copy. The client then merges per entity and field and retries. When both sides changed the same field, the local change wins. A deletion only applies to an entity the other side has not touched.
    • A save that would drop most of a large workspace is refused with 422, unless it is a deliberate load or replace.
    • Every write first keeps the previous revision in the history. Postgres keeps it in flygon_flow_workspace_history; without Postgres it goes to BACKUP_DIR/workspaces/history/.
    • Open tabs pick up remote changes every 20 seconds, and offline edits upload when the connection comes back.

    API writes go through the same revision check, so an agent's change and a human's edit never silently overwrite each other.

    Sharing

    The owner of an environment can share part of it with another Flow user, by email: a person and everything below them, hand-picked cards, a project, a DevOps label, or the whole environment. The Share dialog (a card's Share… button, or Settings › Environment › Share this environment…) shows a live preview of exactly what the other person will see. Permissions are view, comment or edit.

    The recipient finds it under Settings › Sharing › Shared with you and adds it to one of their own environments. The shared cards appear there as linked boxes with their own layout. Direct co-owners of a shared card show as read-only name stubs, and nothing else of theirs is shared. Edits travel both ways as the permission allows. Revoking a share removes everything from the recipient's environment. Recipients cannot share further; instead they ask the owner, who approves or denies the request.

    The server enforces all of this: linked copies are computed from the owner's data on every read and are never stored in the recipient's environment. The API, the CLI and MCP see each environment's own data only. Details: docs/sharing.md.

    The owner can also invite people to the app itself (Settings › Account › Invite to Flow). The invited person signs in with that email and gets their own empty environment.

    Versioning

    Flygon Flow uses Bradshaw Versioning. Every commit that reaches main gets the next YEAR.MONTH.UPDATE:

    • The year is zero-based from 2026, so October 2026 is 0.10.x and January 2027 is 1.1.x. Months are calendar months, in the America/Phoenix timezone.
    • The registry is public/devlog.json. Each release records its version, commit, admission time and compatibility (compatible, action-required or breaking, with the required action), plus any verified deployments.
    • A version identifies source code only. It says nothing about whether that code is deployed.

    These docs are generated from the same registry, so the version in the header is the newest recorded release.

    AgentFlow

    AgentFlow is an org chart for agentic work. You lay out the agents that do work for a business, say what each one is for and what it takes in and produces, chain them into workflows, and tie them to the projects, DevOps cards and deadlines they own.

    Flow stores the design. It does not run agents itself. A runner of your choice (an agent harness, a home server, a cron job) reads an agent's or workflow's brief through the API or MCP and does the work, then reports back on the DevOps cards like anyone else.

    Agents

    An agent has name, kind, title, status, live, reportsTo, supervisor, purpose, instructions, runtime, models[], model, auto, schedule, inputs[], outputs[], tools[], an optional job, and links projects[], cards[], items[].

    • kind: agent (an AI agent), human, team (a group heading in the org) or automation (a scripted job without AI, such as a backup timer, that runs on its own schedule outside Flow; see Automations).
    • schedule says when it runs, in plain words or cron, such as "Weekdays 09:00" or 30 22 * * * ("" for none). For an AI agent, its runner starts it then.
    • job is {runner, id}: the runner job it was promoted from (see Scheduled jobs). It is absent when there is none; send null or "" to agents.update to clear it.
    • status: draft, active, paused or retired.
    • reportsTo is another agent. Together these form the AgentFlow org chart. An agent cannot report to itself or to anyone below it (reports_loop). A saved loop is broken when the workspace loads.
    • supervisor is a person card on one of your mind maps: the human accountable for the agent. A human agent shows a person's photo: its supervisor's, else that of the only person card with the agent's name, else your account photo when the agent has your account name and no person card does.
    • inputs, outputs and tools are short text lists, such as "A card in Doing" or "Pull request linked on the card".
    • instructions holds the system prompt or runbook. runtime says where it runs (a runner's name).
    • models lists the models it may run on, up to 10 ids from its runner, in order: the primary first, then fallbacks the runner tries when one fails (a rate or usage limit, a provider that is down). model is always the first of them, kept for older runners; sending model alone to agents.update sets models to just it, and when both are sent models wins.
    • auto turns models into a pool: the runner picks one per card instead of always starting on the first. The org card shows Auto (N models), or the primary model and +N for its fallbacks.
    • live is the switch runners obey. It is off for every new agent, and a runner leaves an agent that is not live alone, whatever its status. Turn it on in the agent's side panel, or with agents.update (live: true). The org card then shows a Live badge, in amber when its runner would skip it (no runner or model picked, or a model its runner did not report).
    • Deleting an agent moves its direct reports up to its manager, and its workflow steps become unassigned.

    Runners

    A runner is a machine or service that runs agents, such as a home server with agent harnesses installed. It tells Flow what it can run with runners.report: its name and the models it offers, each with an id, a label and optionally a provider to group it under (such as "Claude" or "OpenCode") and billing: included (covered by a subscription, or free) or metered (paid per use). runners.list returns them. In an agent's side panel, Runs on suggests the reported runners and Models that runner's models, and every org card shows where the agent runs and on which model. Reporting the same models again saves nothing, so a runner can report on every pass.

    flow runners report --input '{"runner":"Home server","models":[{"id":"claudeAgent:claude-sonnet-5-5","label":"Claude · Sonnet 5.5","provider":"Claude","billing":"included"}]}'

    tools/agent-runner.mjs is a reference runner for T3 Code: it reports the providers and models signed in on its machine, and for each live agent whose runtime is its name, starts a T3 thread on the agent's model for the top card in its queue, then moves the card to UAT when the thread finishes. If a model will not start, or its thread fails or hits a limit, it starts the card again on the next model and keeps every attempt; when all have failed it leaves the card and logs it. For an auto agent it prefers included models over metered ones, keeping the pool's order, and can ask a small "router" model to choose among the included ones from the card and the agent's purpose. It marks Claude, Codex, Cursor, Grok and Antigravity models included, OpenCode's own free models (opencode/…) included and other OpenCode models metered, and its settings can override that. It starts in dry-run mode, so it only prints what it would do until you turn that off. See the comment at the top of the file for its settings.

    Scheduled jobs

    A runner can also tell Flow which scheduled jobs it found: systemd timers, crontab lines, scheduled T3 or Claude tasks, Vercel or Railway crons, GitHub Actions schedules, Windows scheduled tasks. It sends them as jobs in the same runners.report call, up to 500 per runner:

    Field
    idRequired, up to 200 characters, stable per runner, e.g. systemd:backup.timer or vercel:my-app:/api/cron/sync.
    nameUp to 120 characters (defaults to the id).
    sourceWhere it is scheduled, up to 40 characters: systemd, cron, t3, vercel, railway, aside, windows, claude, github or other (the default). Other text is kept as it is.
    groupA display group, up to 120 characters, e.g. "Home server" or "Vercel · my-app".
    scheduleWhen, in words, up to 200 characters: "Daily 22:30", "Every 5 min".
    cronThe cron expression, when there is one (up to 120).
    commandA short summary of what it runs (up to 300).
    aitrue when the job starts an AI agent.
    enabledfalse when it is switched off on the runner (default true).
    lastRun, nextRunISO times.
    lastStatusok, failed, running or unknown (the default).

    jobs replaces the stored list. Leave it out to keep the stored jobs, or send [] to clear them. To keep writes down, a report is not saved when the only changes are lastRun and nextRun, unless the jobs were last saved six hours ago or more. A changed lastStatus, a job added or removed, or any other field always saves. The runner's jobsReported is when its jobs were last saved, and the response's changed says whether this report was.

    flow runners report --input '{"runner":"Home server","models":[],"jobs":[{"id":"systemd:backup.timer","name":"Nightly backup","source":"systemd","group":"Home server","schedule":"Daily 22:30","cron":"30 22 * * *","command":"restic backup /srv","lastStatus":"ok","lastRun":"2026-11-01T22:30:00Z","nextRun":"2026-11-02T22:30:00Z"}]}'

    In the app, Scheduled in the org chart's toolbar opens a tray on the left of the canvas. It lists every runner's jobs by runner and group, each with its source icon, name, schedule and a dot for the last run (green OK, red failed, grey unknown). Hover the dot for the last and next run. A group with more than eight jobs starts collapsed to a chip such as "59 jobs" that opens it. Search filters the tray too. Whether the tray is open, and which groups you opened or closed, is remembered on this device.

    Promoting a job

    To put a job in the org, do one of these:

    • Drag the job onto an agent's card. It becomes that agent's report.
    • Drag it onto empty canvas to place it at the top level, right there.
    • Click Promote on the row (top level).
    • Right-click it and choose Promote to org, or Promote under the selected agent.

    The new agent is selected and its side panel opens. Undo removes it again. A job without AI becomes an automation, and an ai job becomes an AI agent whose runtime is the runner (pick its models, then switch it to Live). Either way the agent is named after the job, its role comes from the source (such as "Vercel cron" or "systemd timer"), its schedule is the job's (or its cron line), its purpose is the command, and its status is Active, or Paused when the job is disabled. It is never live, and job links it back. A job is promoted once: its row then shows Promoted (click it to select the agent), and promoting it again selects the agent it already became.

    Automations

    An automation (kind: "automation") is a scripted job in the org with no AI in it. It runs on its own schedule, outside Flow, so it has no runner, no models and no Live switch: live is always false, and a runner never works it. Its card is shorter and grey, with a gear, and shows its schedule (and its job's last status) where an AI agent's card shows its runner and model. Its side panel has a Schedule section with the schedule, and, when it came from a runner job, that job's source, schedule, cron line, command and last and next run (read-only, as the runner reports them). An AI agent's schedule is under Runs on, and its card shows a small clock when it has one.

    The brief lists Schedule: … and Promoted from: <runner> · <job name> under Runtime.

    Workflows

    A workflow has name, description, status, trigger, schedule, steps[{agent, action, output}] and the same links. trigger is manual, schedule or event. schedule says when or on what in plain words, e.g. "Weekdays at 09:00" or "A card enters UAT". Steps run in order, and each one names the agent that handles it.

    Delegation and the work queue

    Delegating a DevOps card to an agent puts it in that agent's work queue. The person on the card stays accountable; the agent does the work. Delegate in the card's Delegated to picker, from the agent's side panel (Cards), or with cards.update (agents: ["Researcher"]; [] clears it). Cards show their agents as square badges, and the board's Agents filter shows one agent's cards. A card can be delegated to several agents.

    agents.work returns everything a runner needs in one call: the agent, its brief, and its queue, which holds the open delegated cards. The queue is ordered Doing, Requests / Sprinted, Blocked, UAT, then the backlogs, and by soonest due date and #number within each. columns: ["doing","requests"] keeps only the cards it can act on now. A runner loop on any machine looks like this:

    1. agents.work with the agent's name and columns: ["doing","requests"]. 2. Take the first card. Move it to Doing with cards.move if it is new. 3. Do the work, following the brief and the card's description and checklist. 4. Report back with cards.update (tick the checklist, add the pull request under links), then cards.move to uat for a human to approve.

    A runner only works agents with live on: agents.list with live: true gives it that list.

    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLOW_TOKEN" "$FLOW_URL/api/v1/envs/$FLOW_ENV/agents/Researcher/work?columns=doing,requests"
flow agents work --input '{"agent":"Researcher","columns":["doing","requests"]}'   # or the agents_work MCP tool

    The runner only calls out to Flow and never needs to be reachable itself, so it works from a home server behind a router.

    Briefs

    agents.get and workflows.get return a brief: Markdown with everything a runner needs. That covers purpose, reporting line, inputs, outputs, tools, runtime, workflow steps, linked projects, cards (open ones from linked projects too) and deadlines, and the instructions. In the app, Copy brief in the side panel puts the same text on the clipboard.

    In the app

    The AgentFlow tab has two views: Org chart (1) and Workflows (2). Scheduled opens the tray of runner jobs (see Scheduled jobs). The org chart is a canvas like the MindMap: drag empty space to pan, scroll to zoom, drag a card to move it (Shift: with its reports), and drag the dot under a card onto another agent to make that agent report to it, or onto empty space to add a new report. Each AI agent's card shows small icons for the makers of its models in the bottom-right corner (the primary first, then up to two fallbacks and "+N"), or one auto symbol with a count when it is on Auto, and its supervisor's face sits on the corner of its avatar. Double-click empty space to add an agent. Tidy up returns to the automatic tree. In the tree, a manager's reports that have no reports of their own are stacked in indented columns (up to six per column) once there are three or more, so a large team stays compact and no reporting lines cross. Positions are saved as the agent's optional x and y. An agent without them, such as one added through the API, is placed under its manager, below the last of its teammates. N adds an agent under the selected one, W adds a workflow, / searches, F fits the org, arrow keys nudge the selected agent. Right-click (or the menu key) opens a menu on an agent, a reporting line, a workflow card or empty canvas: change kind, status or manager, add the agent to a workflow, open its work queue on the DevOps board, duplicate a workflow, and so on. Start from a template creates a small example org and workflow to edit. A DevOps card's detail shows the agents linked to it, and you can assign agents from there.
